qs.q: Which chromosomal translocation is pathognomonic of chronic myeloid leukaemia?
qs.e: This is the Philadelphia chromosome, producing the BCR-ABL fusion gene that defines CML. The other options are characteristic translocations of specific AML/ALL subtypes, not CML.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man presents with fatigue, weight loss and splenomegaly. His full blood count shows WCC 140 × 10⁹/L with marked neutrophilia, left shift and basophilia. Which investigation is required to confirm the diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukaemia?
o: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with cytogenetic analysis
Peripheral blood smear examination and complete blood count only
Quantitative RT-PCR analysis for BCR-ABL fusion gene transcripts
Molecular JAK2 V617F mutation screening and allele quantification
qs.e: Marrow examination with cytogenetics confirms the Philadelphia chromosome, establishing the definitive CML diagnosis alongside molecular BCR-ABL testing.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia (CML) is a clonal myeloproliferative disorder driven by the BCR‑ABL1 fusion gene. It presents with progressive leukocytosis and may evolve from chronic phase to blast crisis if untreated.

sections.p: CML is defined by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creating BCR‑ABL1, causing uncontrolled tyrosine‑kinase activity. Diagnosis requires confirming the fusion gene and a characteristic leukaemoid picture.

t.b: Positive confirms CML; negative prompts alternative diagnoses
Marked leukocytosis with myeloid precursors, basophils, metamyelocytes

sections.p: CML is staged by disease phase: chronic, accelerated, or blast crisis, based on blood counts, blast percentage, and cytogenetic evolution.
b: Accelerated: 10‑19% blasts, rising basophils, cytogenetic instability
Blast crisis: ≥20% blasts, resembles acute leukaemia

sections.p: The primary cause is the BCR‑ABL1 fusion; secondary contributors include exposure to ionising radiation and rare familial predisposition. In low‑resource settings, co‑infection with HIV may accelerate progression.
Patients often feel fatigued, have early satiety from splenomegaly, and may notice bruising or night sweats. Laboratory tests reveal marked leukocytosis with a left shift.
Tests are chosen to confirm the genetic lesion, assess disease burden, and rule out mimics.

t.b: Detects fusion transcript; decreasing levels indicate treatment response
Leukocytosis >100 ×10⁹/L, left shift, basophilia; guides phase assessment
Confirms blast percentage, fibrosis; essential if peripheral data ambiguous
Low LAP typical for CML; normal/high suggests reactive cause

t.a: If PCR unavailable, perform conventional karyotype
t.b: Shows t(9;22) in >90% of cases; less sensitive for low‑level disease

sections.p: Progression to accelerated phase or blast crisis dramatically increases mortality and requires urgent therapy change.
First‑line therapy is a BCR‑ABL1 tyrosine‑kinase inhibitor (TKI). Supportive care addresses cytopenias and splenomegaly. Allogeneic stem‑cell transplant is reserved for TKI failure or blast crisis.
b: Imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib – inhibit BCR‑ABL1, halt proliferation
Hydroxyurea for rapid leukoreduction before TKI start
Avoid interferon due to higher toxicity
Consider transplant if resistant or in blast phase

sections.p: Monitor BCR‑ABL1 transcript levels every 3 months to assess molecular response. Vaccinate against hepatitis B and influenza; counsel on adherence.
b: PCR monitoring for major molecular response

sections.p: Other myeloproliferative or reactive conditions can mimic CML.
Certain labs may appear normal early, leading to delayed diagnosis.
b: Low basophil count early in disease may mask CML
Normal LAP in early chronic phase can be misread as reactive

whenToSeekHelp: Bleeding or bruising with falling platelet count

faq.q: Why is the Philadelphia chromosome pathognomonic for CML?
faq.a: It creates the BCR‑ABL1 tyrosine‑kinase that drives uncontrolled myeloid proliferation, seen in >95% of CML cases.
TKI therapy can achieve long‑term remission; cure is rare, but many patients live normal lives with sustained molecular response.

faq.q: What distinguishes blast crisis from acute leukaemia?
faq.a: Blast crisis arises from pre‑existing CML and retains the BCR‑ABL1 fusion, whereas de‑novo acute leukaemia lacks this hallmark.
